*Apply-the-tool track · Job A.*

Before you trust a single fairness number on a real scorecard, you owe yourself
one thing: **proof the metrics do what they claim**.  This lab builds one
*validation routine* — run every fairness metric, compare it to a gap you already
know, record the error — on a toy whose answer is closed-form, then carries that
**same routine, unchanged**, up the ladder until it is reading a real income
model.  Only the data grows up under it.

**What you will produce:** a calibration sheet — for each fairness metric, its
bias and the regime where it is trustworthy — a vetted toolkit to hand to [Job B
(neutralize an income model)](lab-jobB-neutralize-credit.qmd).

---

## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer

Start where the truth is not in doubt.  `datasets.credit_scores_by_group(gap=g)`
builds a controllable group gap into the data: the latent score is
$\text{latent} \sim \mathcal N(g\cdot\text{group},\,1)$ and the prediction is
$\hat y = \mathbb 1[\text{sigmoid}(\text{latent}) > 0.5] = \mathbb 1[\text{latent} > 0]$.
That makes the **demographic-parity gap** closed-form: with
$P(\hat y = 1 \mid \text{group}=g') = \Phi(g\cdot g')$,

$$
\text{DP gap} = \bigl|P(\hat y{=}1\mid \text{group}{=}1) - P(\hat y{=}1\mid \text{group}{=}0)\bigr|
            = \Phi(g) - \Phi(0) = \Phi(g) - \tfrac12 .
$$

The dependence metrics — measures of how much the prediction and the group move
together — pin down the *direction*: `cka_linear(ŷ, group)` and
`hsic_rbf(ŷ, group)` must **keep rising** as we widen the built-in gap, and an
independent control (`gap=0`, where prediction and group are unrelated) must read
**≈ 0** on all three.  Between them they fix a target for every tool we carry.

**The validation routine — one template, every metric.**  A check is always the
same three steps: run the metric, subtract the known target, flag whether the
error clears a tolerance.  Spelled out once here, reused on every rung above:

```{python}
def validate(name: str, estimate: float, target: float, tol: float) -> dict:
    """Run-compare-record: one row of the calibration sheet.

    error = |estimate − target|        [same units as the metric]
    pass  = error < tol                (tolerance set by the metric's noise floor)
    """
    err = abs(estimate - target)
    return dict(measure=name, target=target, estimate=estimate,
                error=err, ok=err < tol)


def print_sheet(rows: list[dict]) -> None:
    """Pretty-print a list of validate() rows as a calibration table."""
    print(f"{'metric':<24s}{'target':>9s}{'estimate':>10s}{'error':>9s}  pass?")
    print("-" * 58)
    for r in rows:
        mark = "✓" if r["ok"] else "✗"
        print(f"{r['measure']:<24s}{r['target']:>+9.3f}{r['estimate']:>+10.3f}"
              f"{r['error']:>9.3f}    {mark}")
```

The fairness metrics share one shape — every one measures how strongly the
prediction depends on the group, $\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, \text{group})$ — so we
read them off a single helper.  CKA (centered kernel alignment) is just HSIC scaled
to sit between 0 and 1, and it uses the **same double-centering** the dependence
chapter used for distance correlation, written here with the axes visible (the
matrix $H = I - \tfrac1n \mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top$ subtracts the row, column, and
grand means in one stroke):

```{python}
def dp_gap(yhat: Float[Array, "n"], group: Float[Array, "n"]) -> float:
    """Demographic-parity gap = |P(ŷ=1 | g=1) − P(ŷ=1 | g=0)|  [probability units]."""
    return float(abs(yhat[group == 1].mean() - yhat[group == 0].mean()))


def double_centered(v: Float[Array, "n"]) -> Float[Array, "n n"]:
    """Centered Gram matrix HKH for a 1-D variable — the CKA/HSIC core.

    Kᵢⱼ = vᵢ·vⱼ                          (linear kernel)
    (HKH)ᵢⱼ = Kᵢⱼ − K̄ᵢ. − K̄.ⱼ + K̄..      (row, column, grand means removed)
    """
    K: Float[Array, "n n"] = einx.multiply("i, j -> i j", v, v)   # Kᵢⱼ = vᵢ·vⱼ — linear-kernel Gram
    row: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.mean("i j -> i", K)             # K̄ᵢ.
    col: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.mean("i j -> j", K)             # K̄.ⱼ

    Kc: Float[Array, "n n"] = einx.subtract("i j, i -> i j", K, row)   # remove row mean
    Kc = einx.subtract("i j, j -> i j", Kc, col)                       # remove column mean
    return Kc + K.mean()                                              # add back the grand mean K̄..


# CKA_lin is the normalized alignment of the two centered Grams — verify the identity:
g_check = datasets.credit_scores_by_group(n=600, gap=1.6, seed=0)
yh: Float[Array, "n"] = (g_check["score"] > 0.5).astype(float)   # ŷ = 𝟙[score > ½]
gr: Float[Array, "n"] = g_check["group"].astype(float)

Hy: Float[Array, "n n"] = double_centered(yh)
Hg: Float[Array, "n n"] = double_centered(gr)

# CKA_lin = ⟨HKₐH, HK_bH⟩ / (‖HKₐH‖·‖HK_bH‖)   — normalized Gram alignment
align = float((Hy * Hg).sum() / np.sqrt((Hy * Hy).sum() * (Hg * Hg).sum()))
print(f"⟨HKₐH, HK_bH⟩ / ‖·‖‖·‖  = {align:.4f}")
print(f"cka_linear(ŷ, group)    = {cka_linear(yh, gr):.4f}")
```

Now the calibration sweep.  We build in four gaps, compare the measured DP gap
against its closed-form value $\Phi(g) - \tfrac12$, and confirm CKA / HSIC climb
with the gap.  Because we measure on a finite sample, the DP gap jitters a little
around its true value, so we allow a slightly looser tolerance than the exact
formula would suggest:

```{python}
gaps = [0.0, 0.8, 1.6, 2.4]
rung1_rows = []
ck_track, hs_track = [], []                          # to confirm monotone climb
for g in gaps:
    d = datasets.credit_scores_by_group(n=6000, gap=g, seed=0)
    yhat: Float[Array, "n"] = (d["score"] > 0.5).astype(float)   # ŷ = 𝟙[score > ½]
    grp: Float[Array, "n"] = d["group"].astype(float)

    dp = dp_gap(yhat, grp)                            # DP gap uses ALL rows (cheap)
    target = norm.cdf(g) - 0.5                        # closed form Φ(g) − ½
    rung1_rows.append(validate(f"DP gap(g={g:.1f})", dp, target, tol=0.05))

    ck_track.append(cka_linear(yhat[:1500], grp[:1500]))   # subsample O(n²) kernels
    hs_track.append(hsic_rbf(yhat[:1500], grp[:1500]))

print_sheet(rung1_rows)
```

The independent control and the monotonicity claim — both must hold for the
metrics to mean anything:

```{python}
ctrl = datasets.credit_scores_by_group(n=6000, gap=0.0, seed=1)   # a *second* gap=0 draw
yc: Float[Array, "n"] = (ctrl["score"] > 0.5).astype(float)[:1500]   # ŷ subsample — O(n²) kernels
gc: Float[Array, "n"] = ctrl["group"].astype(float)[:1500]

control_rows = [
    validate("CKA control (g=0)",  cka_linear(yc, gc),  0.0, tol=0.02),
    validate("HSIC control (g=0)", hsic_rbf(yc, gc),    0.0, tol=0.01),
]
print_sheet(control_rows)

ck_mono = all(np.diff(ck_track) > -1e-3)             # CKA non-decreasing in the gap
hs_mono = all(np.diff(hs_track) > -1e-3)             # HSIC non-decreasing in the gap
print(f"\nCKA  across gaps: {[f'{c:.3f}' for c in ck_track]}   monotone↑: {ck_mono}")
print(f"HSIC across gaps: {[f'{h:.3f}' for h in hs_track]}   monotone↑: {hs_mono}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-rung1-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Rung 1 calibration. Left: the demographic-parity gap tracks its closed-form target Φ(g) − ½ along the diagonal (points on the dashed identity line ⇒ unbiased) — it saturates toward ½ as the built-in gap grows, exactly as Φ does. Right: linear CKA and RBF HSIC both climb monotonically with the built-in gap and collapse to ≈ 0 at g = 0 (the independent control), so a fairness number near zero genuinely means 'no group dependence,' not a blind spot."
dp_hat: Float[Array, "n_gaps"] = np.array([r["estimate"] for r in rung1_rows])
dp_tgt: Float[Array, "n_gaps"] = np.array([r["target"]   for r in rung1_rows])

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.2))

ax0.plot([0, 0.5], [0, 0.5], "--", c=INK, lw=1.0)        # identity = unbiased
ax0.scatter(dp_tgt, dp_hat, s=70, c=COOL, zorder=3)
ax0.set_xlabel("target  Φ(g) − ½"); ax0.set_ylabel("measured DP gap")
ax0.set_title("DP gap recovers Φ(g) − ½", fontsize=11); despine(ax0)

ax1.plot(gaps, ck_track, "-o", c=COOL, label="CKA (linear)")
ax1.plot(gaps, np.array(hs_track) * 10, "-o", c=WARM, label="HSIC × 10")
ax1.axhline(0.0, ls=":", c=INK, lw=0.8)
ax1.set_xlabel("built-in group gap g"); ax1.set_ylabel("dependence metric")
ax1.set_title("CKA, HSIC climb with the gap", fontsize=11)
ax1.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(ax1)

fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Every target is met within its tolerance: the DP gap is an unbiased estimate of
the closed-form $\Phi(g)-\tfrac12$, the dependence metrics rise monotonically with
the gap and vanish on the independent control.  That `validate` routine is now
frozen — **we never rewrite it; we only feed it harder data.**

## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market

A simple on/off toy gap is the easy case.  What actually bites a real scorecard is
a **proxy that leaks the sensitive variable through a curve** — a feature that
sneaks the group back in even after you drop it — and `datasets.fair_regression()`
builds exactly that, with the structure known in advance.  Its target is
$y = 0.6x + 0.7S + 0.7(S^2-1) + \varepsilon$: a *straight-line* leak through $S$
**and** a *curved* leak through $S^2$.  Drop $S$ and remove only the straight-line
part, and the metrics must split — the linear ones (DP gap, `cka_linear`) read
$\approx 0$ while the kernel ones (`cka_rbf`, `hsic_rbf`) still fire on the
leftover $S^2$ dependence.  We feed all three predictions to the *same* `validate`
routine and confirm each metric reports the structure we built in.

```{python}
d = datasets.fair_regression(n=600, seed=7)
x: Float[Array, "n"] = d["x"]
S: Float[Array, "n"] = d["s"]
y: Float[Array, "n"] = d["y"]
# ground truth: y = 0.6 x + 0.7 S + 0.7 (S² − 1) + noise  — linear AND curved leak

# plain model (uses S), then two neutralizers of its prediction
Phi: Float[Array, "n p"] = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x, S, S**2 - 1.0])   # design matrix Φ
theta: Float[Array, "p"]
theta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Phi, y, rcond=None)
plain: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.dot("n p, p -> n", Phi, theta)   # ŷ = Φθ

# β = Cov(ŷ, S)/Var(S);  residual = ŷ − β·S
beta = np.cov(plain, S)[0, 1] / np.var(S)
lin: Float[Array, "n"] = plain - beta * S                 # LINEAR removal: kills the line
cka_neut: Float[Array, "n"] = fair_fit(x, y, S, mu=8.0)   # KERNEL penalty: kills line + curve


def dep_row(name: str, p: Float[Array, "n"], metric, target: float, tol: float) -> dict:
    """One validate() row for a dependence metric of prediction p on S."""
    return validate(name, metric(p, S), target, tol)
```

The plain model leaks on *every* metric (it is using $S$).  Linear removal
subtracts the best straight-line fit of the prediction on $S$ — the slope $\beta$
is just how much the prediction shifts per unit of $S$ — so it kills the line, but
the curve survives in the kernel metrics.  The kernel penalty closes both.  Each is
a known target:

```{python}
leak_rows = [
    # plain — leaks everywhere (uses S): high on all three
    dep_row("plain  cka_lin",  plain,    cka_linear, 0.25, tol=0.15),
    dep_row("plain  cka_rbf",  plain,    cka_rbf,    0.25, tol=0.15),
    # linear removal — line gone (cka_lin≈0) but the S² CURVE survives (cka_rbf high)
    dep_row("lin-rm cka_lin",  lin,      cka_linear, 0.00, tol=0.05),
    dep_row("lin-rm cka_rbf",  lin,      cka_rbf,    0.18, tol=0.12),  # leak survives
    # kernel penalty — line AND curve gone: all near zero
    dep_row("kernel cka_rbf",  cka_neut, cka_rbf,    0.00, tol=0.05),
    dep_row("kernel hsic",     cka_neut, hsic_rbf,   0.00, tol=0.01),
]
print_sheet(leak_rows)
print(f"\nlinear removal: cka_lin={cka_linear(lin, S):.3f} (line gone) but "
      f"cka_rbf={cka_rbf(lin, S):.3f} — the S² leak survives the linear drop.")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-rung2-leak
#| fig-cap: "The S²-proxy leak, and which metric catches it. Each panel is the prediction against the sensitive S. Plain (left) bends hard with S — every metric reads high. Linear removal (center) flattens the *tilt* but leaves the curve: cka_lin ≈ 0 yet cka_rbf still sees the bend. The kernel penalty (right) flattens line and curve together. The validation routine confirms each metric reports exactly the structure left behind."
preds = [("plain (uses S)", plain), ("linear removal", lin), ("kernel penalty (μ=8)", cka_neut)]
cols = [COOL, CRASH, plotting.PALETTE["green"]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12.5, 3.9), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, p), col in zip(axes, preds, cols):
    ax.scatter(S, p, s=8, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
    annotate_box(ax, 0.04, 0.96,
                 f"cka_lin={cka_linear(p, S):.2f}\ncka_rbf={cka_rbf(p, S):.2f}",
                 ha="left", va="top")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11); ax.set_xlabel("sensitive S")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
axes[0].set_ylabel("prediction")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The split checks out exactly as designed: the linear metrics go silent the moment
the tilt is removed, while the kernel metrics keep firing until the *curve* is
gone too.  The routine did not change; only the data did, and it still reads the
truth we planted — a metric "passes" only on the dependence shape it can see.

## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket

Now the real panel.  We **reload** the prepared income table — there is no
cleaning here; the ACS (American Community Survey) decode + filter pipeline and the
$(X, y, s)$ handoff live in
[the credit-dataset primer](../../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd) — split it into
target / sensitive attribute / proxy features, and confirm the metrics stay
*well-behaved* on a real scorecard.  **What we are looking for:** on real data we
have no built-in gap to compare against, so instead we check that each metric obeys
the **properties** a sane fairness metric must have — stays in range $[0,1]$ (CKA)
or non-negative (HSIC), reads $\approx 0$ when we neutralize a score against itself,
and only ever **falls** as we turn the neutrality knob $\mu$ up.  If a metric
breaks any of these, we cannot trust the number it reports where the truth is
hidden.

```{python}
credit = datasets.load_credit()                       # real US Census ACSIncome panel
y_real: Float[Array, "n"] = credit["income_high"].to_numpy().astype(float)   # target: 1 if income > $50k
s_real: Float[Array, "n"] = credit["sex"].to_numpy().astype(float)           # protected: 1 = male
X_real = credit.drop(columns=["income_high", "sex"])      # proxies (DataFrame) — sex DROPPED

# the one allowed lab-local step: one-hot the categoricals (a modelling choice)
X_enc: Float[Array, "n d"] = pd.get_dummies(X_real, columns=["occupation", "marital"],
                                            drop_first=True).to_numpy().astype(float)
print(f"{len(credit):,} rows × {X_enc.shape[1]} proxy features   "
      f"(target rate {y_real.mean():.0%}, male rate {s_real.mean():.0%})")
```

A scorecard that *drops* `sex` still leaks it through `occupation` — the model
never sees sex directly, yet occupation carries enough of it to reconstruct the
group.  We fit one, then take **one** lab-local step — subsample ~1500 rows for the
O($n^2$) kernel metrics, which would be too slow on the full table — and feed the
real score to the *same* `validate` routine, now checking each invariant.  The key
numbers to watch are the DP gap and the two kernel metrics: a non-zero reading here
is the leak showing through.

```{python}
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X_enc, y_real)   # scorecard, sex dropped
prob: Float[Array, "n"] = clf.predict_proba(X_enc)[:, 1]     # continuous score P(income > $50k)
yhat: Float[Array, "n"] = (prob > 0.5).astype(float)         # ŷ = 𝟙[score > ½]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx: Float[Array, "m"] = rng.choice(len(y_real), 1500, replace=False)   # subsample for O(n²) kernels
pk: Float[Array, "m"] = prob[idx]
sk: Float[Array, "m"] = s_real[idx]

# Invariant 1 — every metric lands inside its valid range, and the leak is real.
gap0 = dp_gap(yhat, s_real)
range_rows = [
    validate("DP gap ∈ [0,1]",  gap0,             0.5, tol=0.5),   # ∈ [0,1]
    validate("cka_rbf ∈ [0,1]", cka_rbf(pk, sk),  0.5, tol=0.5),
    validate("hsic ≥ 0",        hsic_rbf(pk, sk), 0.5, tol=0.5),
]
print(f"scorecard (sex dropped):  DP gap={gap0:.3f}   "
      f"cka_rbf={cka_rbf(pk, sk):.3f}   hsic={hsic_rbf(pk, sk):.4f}")
print_sheet(range_rows)
```

```{python}
# Invariant 2 — neutralized self-control: drive μ high and the metric must vanish.
prob_neut: Float[Array, "n"] = fair_fit(prob, prob, s_real, mu=50.0)   # heavily neutralize the score
self_rows = [
    validate("cka_rbf neutralized", cka_rbf(prob_neut[idx], sk), 0.0, tol=0.02),
    validate("hsic neutralized",    hsic_rbf(prob_neut[idx], sk), 0.0, tol=0.01),
]
print_sheet(self_rows)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-rung3-monotone-compute
# Invariant 3 — sweep the neutrality knob μ and watch every metric fall.
mus = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 8.0, 30.0]
ck_curve, hs_curve, dp_curve = [], [], []
for mu in mus:
    p: Float[Array, "n"] = fair_fit(prob, prob, s_real, mu=mu)   # neutralize score vs sex
    ck_curve.append(cka_rbf(p[idx], sk))                         # curved+linear dependence on S
    hs_curve.append(hsic_rbf(p[idx], sk))
    dp_curve.append(dp_gap((p > 0.5).astype(float), s_real))     # group-rate disparity

# monotone↓: each metric is non-increasing as μ rises (Δmetric < 0)
mono = all(np.diff(ck_curve) < 1e-3) and all(np.diff(dp_curve) < 1e-3)
print(f"monotone↓ in μ:  CKA {[f'{c:.3f}' for c in ck_curve]}   ok: {mono}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-rung3-monotone
#| fig-cap: "Real-scorecard sanity, Invariant 3: turning up the neutrality knob μ drives every fairness metric monotonically down. As the kernel penalty removes more of the score's dependence on sex, CKA, HSIC, and the demographic-parity gap all fall together toward their floors — a knob that *only* trades accuracy for neutrality, never the reverse, exactly what a number you would stake a lending decision on must do."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.2))
ax.plot(mus, np.array(ck_curve) / ck_curve[0], "-o", c=COOL, label="cka_rbf")
ax.plot(mus, np.array(hs_curve) / hs_curve[0], "-o", c=WARM, label="hsic")
ax.plot(mus, np.array(dp_curve) / dp_curve[0], "-o", c=CRASH, label="DP gap")
ax.set_xlabel("neutrality knob μ"); ax.set_ylabel("metric (relative to μ=0)")
ax.set_title("Every fairness metric falls monotonically with μ", fontsize=11.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Where This Data Comes From
The panel, its `(X, y, s)` split, the group gap, and the `occupation` channel
that leaks `sex` even after the drop are laid bare in the data primer —
[The Income & Fairness Dataset](../../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd).  This lab
reloads that prepared table and never re-derives the decode or ACSIncome filter.
:::

Every invariant holds on real data: the metrics stay in range, vanish on a
heavily neutralized score, and fall monotonically as we turn up $\mu$.  We cannot
check a *target* here, but a metric that obeys all three properties is one we can
trust where the truth is hidden.

## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The Calibration Sheet

The deliverable is the **calibration sheet itself**: for each fairness metric, how
far off it ran in our tests (its bias) and the setting where it can be trusted.
This is the vetted toolkit — the page you point to when someone later questions a
number from [Job B (neutralize an income model)](lab-jobB-neutralize-credit.qmd).
Each row sums up what the three rungs proved: the closed-form recovery, the known
blind spot, and the regime to trust.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-calibration-sheet
#| tbl-cap: "The deliverable calibration sheet — every fairness metric's bias and its regime of trust, distilled from the three rungs above."
sheet = [
    ("DP gap",
     "unbiased vs Φ(g) − ½; |error| < 0.05 on the toy",
     "group-rate disparity — needs a THRESHOLD; blind to score shape"),
    ("cka_linear",
     "→ 0 on independent control; = Pearson² on 1-D scores",
     "linear group dependence — BLIND to the S² (curved) proxy leak"),
    ("cka_rbf",
     "→ 0 when neutralized; bounded [0,1], makes μ comparable",
     "curved & linear group dependence; O(n²) — subsample ~1500"),
    ("hsic_rbf",
     "→ 0 under independence; non-negative, unbounded above",
     "same curved coverage as cka_rbf; trust its SIGN/ranking, not scale"),
]
print(f"{'metric':<14s}{'bias / calibration':<48s}regime of trust")
print("=" * 100)
for name, bias, regime in sheet:
    print(f"{name:<14s}{bias:<48s}{regime}")

errs = {
    "DP gap\n(toy)":     np.mean([r["error"] for r in rung1_rows]),
    "CKA\n(control)":    np.mean([r["error"] for r in control_rows if "CKA" in r["measure"]]),
    "cka_rbf\n(neut)":   self_rows[0]["error"],
    "hsic\n(neut)":      self_rows[1]["error"],
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.0))
ax.bar(list(errs), list(errs.values()), color=[INK, COOL, WARM, WARM])
ax.axhline(0.05, ls="--", c=CRASH, lw=1.0, label="0.05 tolerance")
ax.set_ylabel("mean |error| vs known target")
ax.set_title("Calibration errors — all within tolerance", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Read the sheet as a contract.  The **DP gap** is unbiased but needs a threshold
and is blind to where in the score the dependence sits.  **`cka_linear`** is the
cheap, linear-only rung — it goes silent on the curved $S^2$ proxy that real
scorecards leak through, so it is never the last word.  **`cka_rbf`** sees that
curve, is bounded $[0,1]$ so $\mu$ is interpretable, and vanishes on a neutralized
score, at an O($n^2$) cost.  **`hsic_rbf`** has the same curved coverage but is
unbounded, so trust its *ranking* of models, not the absolute scale.  Hand this
toolkit to [Job B](lab-jobB-neutralize-credit.qmd) to neutralize a real income
model — every fairness number now backed by a documented bias and a regime of
trust.
